closed-update-refused-by-the-node-the-ne.text: Closed update refused by the node: the negative host follows a closed registry.

A closed registry refuses an update twice. The open-datum executable stops it before anything is built, and the closed-datum validator refuses it on chain. Only the first is shown today. This ticket adds the second to the negative host, the instrument that skips the executable, submits what the executable would never build, and reports what the node itself says. Issue 661, a part of issue 650.

story.text: As the presenter of Demo 1, I can say that a closed-datum update is refused by the application on chain, not only by the executable. Someone who skips the executable and submits an honest controller update anyway sees the node refuse it, and the failing script is closed-datum's spend.

What the presenter shows: a registry created with open-datum create --closed, a key registered in it, then the controller's own update of that key, built by the negative host and submitted with no local evaluation. The node answers with a refusal, and the refusal names the registry's own application script in the spending role. In the same registry, on the same key, the controller's termination is accepted: the node refuses the update and nothing else. The scene is rehearsed on Saturday 17 October, after the journey of issue 660.

what-is-established.text: Read on main at 38c2e436 on 15 October 2026. Each statement was checked in the source before the plan relied on it.

The negative host builds forbidden transactions, signs them, skips local evaluation, submits them and judges the node's own answer. It finds the application's script hash from the registry it opened, never from a literal (Negative/Submit.hs, applicationHashOf), so a refusal is judged against the registry's own pin.

The host opens a registry in five handlers (insert, update, terminate, withdraw, fold), each through one call that names openDatumApplication (Negative/Run.hs, the five calls to attached). That call loads the code the application value names and resolves the registry against it, refusing when the recorded policy is another derivation. Against a closed registry every host handler therefore stops at that named refusal before it builds anything. The host needs to follow the registry's mode.

The other places that name the open value (Negative/Craft.hs, Negative/Read.hs, and the reads inside Negative/Run.hs) use it for the holding rules and the application address only. The two modes share both: applicationIn differs from the open value in the pin title alone, and liveOutputs ignores its application argument. They need no change.

The executable reads a registry's mode with registryMode and followingMode, exported from Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Run. The two small functions that apply them to a command's arguments (readModeFor, readModeForFold) are not exported.

The part runner builds the open-datum executable and the host from the release archive, creates the registry with open-datum create and judges the node's refusal: the receipt outcome, the failing script's hash against the registry's own pin, the script's role, and an equal read of the registry before and after. The update pairs use an honest controller update as their accepting control. On a closed registry that update is itself what the node refuses, so this part's control is the termination of the same key, as the part for a release outside any fold already does.

Part names are listed in the part runner, in the discovery table (negative/pairs.json), and in the node-free controls. The mutant table (mutants/rules.json) is the second table. The workflow discovers both from the tables, so it needs no new job.

The ruleset lists the aggregator jobs ("Negative host pairs", "Negative host mutants", "Negative host mutant self-check" and the others). The matrix job names are not listed, so this ticket adds no required name. The self-check job runs the no-patch control for the registry mutant only (negative-host.yml:218); it does not grow with the mutant table.
The closed spend refuses an update with the trace closed-datum-update, once in open_datum.ak. The mutant runner checks that a patch removes exactly the lines of its rule's label and touches one file.

Open pull requests that touch the same files: draft 597 edits negative-host.yml (in other places than this change) and flake.nix; draft 662 (the journey of issue 660) names the negative host as not touched.

requirements.text: host-follows-the-registry-mode: each host handler that opens a registry reads its mode from the chain, by the same read the executable uses, and loads the code of that mode. A registry whose mode cannot be read runs exactly as it does today, so the registry's own refusal is what the host reports. The read happens inside the command, where a provider failure is classified as it is today.

open-registries-behave-as-today: on a registry whose recorded policy is the open-datum derivation, every host handler builds, submits and reports what it does today. The thirteen existing parts pass unchanged.

closed-update-is-refused-by-the-closed-spend: the part closed-update creates a registry with open-datum create --closed from the release archive, registers a key and folds it active with the executable, then submits the controller's honest update of that key through the host. The node refuses it: the receipt reports a ledger refusal and exit status 11, the failing script's hash equals the registry's own application pin and its role is the application spending role, and the read of the registry is equal before and after.

refused-script-is-closed-datums: the pin judged is closed-datum's. The create receipt names the application open_datum.closed_datum, and the pin differs from the pin the open-datum application would have for the same seed, which the part reads by previewing the creation of the same seed without the switch. A refusal by the open application's script could not satisfy both.

closed-update-control-is-a-termination: in the same registry, on the same key, the controller books the key's termination and folds it, with the executable. The node accepts both and the key reads as terminal. A refusal for another reason (a wrong key, a broken registry) would fail this control too.

part-lists-agree: the part is named in the discovery table, in the part runner and in the node-free membership control, which asserts fourteen names. A part missing from any of them fails a hosted check.

closed-update-accepted-flips-closed-update: the mutant closed-update-accepted patches closed-datum's spend so that an update is no longer refused but handled by open-datum's update rule. Run by the unchanged mutant runner, it makes the honest update accepted, so closed-update flips, while its control pair still passes. The mutant self-check job also runs the runner's no-patch control for this mutant, which shows that without the patch nothing flips.
existing-mutants-unchanged: the eight existing mutants run as today.

docs-name-the-part-and-the-mutant: docs/negative-host.md names the part in its story and its table, and the mutant, with the counts they change; the page's speech is regenerated by the extraction tool and its changed segments carry clips.
no-lean-statement: by operator ruling the write-once rule has no Lean statement. No document of this change claims otherwise.

registry-and-fences-untouched: no change to the registry contract, its script hashes, the registry library, the singular commands, the validator source, or the files of the wallet-preparation and signing work.
nothing-on-preprod: no part, mutant or command of this ticket reaches preprod.

rulings-in-force.text: Recorded in the words they were given.

No Lean (operator, 15 October 2026): "We do not need lean here. This is just for demo one, and then we decide if to formalize it." The affected story is the presenter's closed registration. The ruling declares a limit: the write-once rule has no Lean statement, theorem, corpus row or simulator case. It does not change any Lean statement and does not permit a rule that contradicts clear Lean: the closed spend reaches every other rule by calling open-datum's handlers.

One application, one flag (operator, 15 October 2026): "make sure you refactor the open datum application enough so that closed datum is just a flag over it." Here the flag is the mode of one application value, and the host follows it.

On chain (desk and epic owner, 15 October 2026): validator closed_datum sits inside open_datum.ak; its spend refuses an update with the trace closed-datum-update, and mint and release delegate to open-datum. Issue 651 delivered it. This ticket consumes it and never edits it: the mutant is a patch applied to a scratch copy.
The mode comes from the chain (operator, 6 October 2026, users have only a page and the chain): no local file decides it.
Required checks (operator, 14 October 2026): a published check is required by default. The part and the mutant run under the existing aggregators, so no new name exists.

decisions-and-what-they-were-chosen-over.text: Decisions and what they were chosen over.

stated-limits.text: The write-once rule has no Lean statement, by ruling.
The refusal is attributed by the failing script's hash and role. The node's reason text is not observed: the deployed validators are compiled without traces.
The part runs on a devnet from the release archive. Nothing runs on preprod.

What the part submits is the host's honest update of a closed registry. That the closed spend refuses a tampered update as well is not claimed: the closed arm refuses every update before any field is read.
Each host command now reads the registry's state output once more before it reads it again.
